newsitem.title: USA: U.S. team isolates sexual behavior gene in flies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. team isolates sexual behavior gene in flies.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Thursday they had isolated a gene that controlled most or all sexual behaviour in male fruit flies.

Scientists from four U.S. universities said their research was the first to pinpoint a single gene that worked in the brain to govern nearly all aspects of a complex sort of behaviour in adult animals.

The findings provide a starting point for a host of other studies to learn how sexual behaviour and sexual orientation are specified by genes and controlled by the nervous system, the researchers said.

The research raises the question of whether human sexual behaviour may be commanded by a single gene. So far, no gene comparable to the one isolated in fruit flies has been found in other species, including humans. But the researchers said they expected scientists to look for such genes.

"Showing that a behaviour as complex as sexual behaviour is controlled by a single gene, at least in flies, raises the obvious possibility that other behaviours will be similarly controlled," said Bruce Baker, professor of biological sciences at Stanford University and one of the four principal investigators for the study.
"Studying such genes may give us insight into the functional organisation of the central nervous system," he added.

The scientists from Stanford, the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Centre at Dallas, Brandeis University and Oregon State University report their findings in the Dec. 13 issue of the journal Cell.

Geneticists have known for years that the gene, called "fruitless" and nicknamed "fru," influences sexual orientation in the fly Drosophila melanogaster, Stanford University said. Male flies with some mutations in the fru gene become bisexual -- they cannot tell other males from female flies when courting.

The geneticists in this study cloned and isolated the fru gene. They showed it was a master gene that controlled not only sexual orientation but all or nearly all the steps in the male fly's elaborate courtship ritual, from its first interest in a female through its rhythmic courting song to its attempts to mate.
They also found the fru gene was part of a group of genes that worked together to govern all aspects of sex in these flies, including the development of male and female organs.

They showed that the gene was at work in a very small fraction of the cells in the fly's brain. The properties of the fru gene's target neurons suggest that they carry out command-and-control functions to set up and coordinate the complex events of male courtship and copulation.
The lead author of the Cell article was Lisa Ryner, a research associate at Stanford. The study was sponsored by the National Institutes of Health.
Now that fru has been cloned, it should have practical uses as a scientific tool, Stanford University said.

It may also prove valuable in agriculture, where some other species of fruit flies destroy crops. It could give pest control experts a reliable way of raising large numbers of sterile insects as birth control to prevent the spread of an infestation of flies, the university said. Stanford and UT Southwestern have applied for a patent on the gene.
